content.confidence: 3: You are fairly confident in your assessment. It is possible that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work. Math/other details were not carefully checked.
content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper considers the shuffle DP model, and the shuffle Gaussian mechanism, where each user has a vector representing their data to send and adds Gaussian noise before sending it to the shuffler. The authors give a closed-form bound for the RDP guarantee of the output of the shuffler, with a few properties that distinguish it from previous bounds: (i) The bound is never worse than the LDP guarantee of the outputs sent to the shuffler, in contrast with past work on shuffle DP, (ii) unlike past analyses of shuffle Gaussians, their bound is computable efficiently (in particular, the time to compute it does not grow exponentially in n; they are able to compute their bound in experiments where n = 60000), (iii) There does not seem to be any slack in the analysis, (iv) the authors extend their bounds to the settings where the users who participate in a round are a uniformly random subsample of fixed size, or where each user opts in with the same probability, resolving open problems posed in recent papers. The authors run experiments on MNIST, showing that their accounting scheme allows them to achieve good accuracy for reasonable epsilons even with the shuffle DP constraint.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
The main strengths of the paper are: that it provides an analysis of a mechanism that is interesting both theoretically and in practice (as partially evidenced by the past work of Gopi et al and Koskela et al., and due to gaps in existing DP accounting libraries as mentioned in the authors), that the analysis is fairly technical yet intuitive, and that the authors provide a fairly complete set of results for the problem being studied (see (i) and (iv) in the summary). 

The main weakness of the paper is that I felt there were some parts of the presentation that were a bit lacking. I felt I needed to reread some parts of the paper multiple times to fully understand what was going on. My main suggestions to the authors for improving the presentation in the paper are:

(1) "Our contributions. In this paper, we provide the first non-trivial privacy guarantee for the shuffle Gaussian mechanism." - as you mention, composition theorems for approximate DP local-randomizers exist and can give some DP guarantee for the shuffle Gaussian mechanism, so either "non-trivial" needs to be spelled out a bit here or you should mention something specific to your guarantee (e.g. RDP vs approx DP) explicitly.

(2) Theorem 1: Renyi divergence is well defined for non-integer orders, but the theorem/paper seems to assume lambda is an integer. As far as I can tell this is pretty necessary for the use of the multinomial theorem in the proof. One can of course use monotonicity of Renyi divergences to justify this assumption (and the bound only worsens by constants), but I think this should be explicitly stated.

(3) Is it possible to briefly mention how long Algorithm 1's implementation takes for some common values of lambda? (e.g. perhaps those in the range commonly used by privacy accounting libraries). I think this is slightly important since one of your main claimed improvements over past work is the efficiency of your algorithm. Here I'm assuming if n >= lambda, which is likely in practice, then n does not substantially affect the runtime besides the time spent on arithmetic; if this is not the case it may be good to clarify this in the paper.

In addition, there are a few open problems the authors mention that could be viewed as weaknesses. The big one is that Theorem 3, for the setting where users opt in randomly, depends on a conjecture the authors have only verified empirically. However, given the amount to which this paper has improved over some past works, and the transparency of the authors with respect to the problems their work leaves open, I do not view these as a strong weakness.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
As mentioned above, I felt that a few points made in the paper needed some rereading to understand, and based on my above suggestions I think there is room for improving the paper. Of course, part of the issue may be that page limits prohibited including some details that would help clarify these parts.However, other parts of the paper are fairly easy to read and understand. I think the materials in the appendix are also pretty thorough at explaining some of the details of the paper. 

As mentioned above, I felt that the quality of the work was strong. The paper is likely to have high practical impact, and addressed a problem that has been of high interest in the community, and does so using a technically strong analysis and good practical suggestions for implementing their accounting scheme. The experiments in the paper do a good job solidifying the potential to use the algorithms from the paper in practice, both in terms of efficiency of running the accounting scheme and achieving accuracy for model training in the shuffle DP setting.

The results in the paper are of course novel since they show DP guarantees that quantitatively and qualitatively have not been shown before, to my knowledge.
content.summary_of_the_review: Overall I support accepting the paper. I think the past works studying the problem, the many open-source libraries for accounting, and the authors experiments/implementations justify the importance and potential impact of the paper. Theoretically the approaches are intuitive but still require a fair amount of technical work. The theoretical results in the paper are the first of their kind in several aspects. Furthermore, the set of theoretical results is fairly robust and complete.
content.correctness: 4: All of the claims and statements are well-supported and correct.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 4: The contributions are significant, and do not exist in prior works.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 3: The contributions are significant and somewhat new. Aspects of the contributions exist in prior work.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper in the shuffle-DP model and in particular, if all the randomizers are using Gaussian mechanism to preserve privacy. Shuffle-DP has gained a lot of attraction recently and the Gaussian mechanism is the to-go privacy (in fact, optimal) mechanism for DP-SGD under an approximate DP guarantee. In the local model, the same can be said about DJW randomizer, that behaves like a subgaussian r.v..
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
The paper gives a bound on the Renyi divergence of shuffled Gaussian mechanism. This, in my opinion, is new result even though not particularly hard to get. The bound is in the term of multinomial coefficients. The authors also give an easy to state corollary, which is exactly the RDP guarantee of a Gaussian mechanism. This is a very lose bound in my understanding (the authors may correct me here). I would believe it is important for the paper to give a comparison with the recent RDP bound on shuffled mechanism by Feldman, McMillan, and Talwar (SODA 2023).

The authors also give an algorithm to numerically evaluate the RDP guarantee of the shuffle-Gaussian mechanism. The main issue is to compute the integer partition, an approximate version of which has been studied extensively in the literature of numerical computation. 

Overall, the results are not surprising. The computation of RDP for the shuffle-Gaussian does not introduce any new technique, but it is a calculation exercise that I would not be surprised if it is one of the assignment questions for advanced graduate course or in the white paper associated with one of the DP implementations. It is a handy result, but I am not sure how novel or significant it is. 

I am looking forward to the conversation with the authors to better understand if I have missed some subtle points in the paper or as to why the analysis is difficult.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
The paper is well written. 
The result in the paper is important in practice considering the application of Gaussian mechanism in DP-SGD.
The novely of the paper is not that much.

content.confidence: 4: You are confident in your assessment, but not absolutely certain. It is unlikely, but not impossible, that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work.
content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper presents a precise expression for computing the RDP of the shuffled Gaussian mechanism. The expression is a binomial computation. They further show that the RDP of the Gaussian mechanism without the shuffler upper bounds the expression presented by them at all values in the RDP curve. They provide some experimental evidence that their presented bounds can provide tighter analysis of DP under shuffling.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths -- 

The expression is useful in the sense that getting RDP bounds for shuffled mechanism DP has potential. The paper is decently written although several parts can use more clarifications. The expression shows that shuffling can lead to better privacy for the Gaussian mechanism for all parameter ranges of interest. 


Weaknesses -- 

While the bound is useful I find the following weaknesses in the result and experimental comparisons presented in the paper. The authors should feel free to clarify any misunderstandings that belie my comments below. 

1. While the expression is useful to know, it is not particularly hard to derive (can be considered in my opinion to be a difficult exercise for a grad class in DP). This by itself is not a dealbreaking aspect by any means and ease of analysis should be appreciated in general, however I could not find an element in the analysis which is revealing or conducive to further future research. Thus I find the novelty/scientic impact of the derivation low. 

2. The expression is still difficult to compute for large n and large lambda. The paper makes a claim that this computation is 'easy', however I disagree that the computation can be efficient in the large scale setting. 

3. I am not fully convinced by the experimental evaluation of the proposed bound's advantages in the various calculations/simulations presented. I detail my questions below

a. Comparison with Feldman et al. Firstly if I understand correctly the presented bound is an equality for the RDP then why is it case that at low amount of compositions the value through their bound is weaker than the Feldman bound. Secondly, I didnt fully understand the protocol of comparison here, they say that they enumerate over all delta, but then the results are shown for what delta, what delta is eventually selected post the enumeration. Lastly the expression for the Feldman bound has some issue in its bracketing, please fix that. 

b. Comparison of shuffled vs central DP -- If i understand correctly the section 'Privacy accounting of DP-SGD' is for the purpose of showing that the under the shuffled model the accuracy loss over central DP-SGD is not that much. However it is hard to understand how 'that much' is to be quantified. While I am not an epxert in this area, I am hard-pressed to believe that there is no comparison in literature of DP-SGD with Shuffled Model DP-SGD through any sort of bounds (say through Feldman et al). Why not include that comparison in the analysis? 

c. Shuffled Check-in Gaussian experiments -- These have to be somewhat discounted in my opinion until the the calculations performed on the assumption of monotonicity is proven. Privacy in my opinion has to be guaranteed by proof and its hard for me to fully endorse the experiments until this is proven.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Clarity is good overall however can use further work as detailed above. 

Quality and Originality is somewhat limited as detailed earlier.
content.summary_of_the_review: Overall it is not the simplicity of the analysis that forms my recommendation. It is the other weaknesses that lead to my recommendation. A novel analysis technique could have offsetted these weaknesses. I am happy to revisit my score based on the authors' clarification.
content.correctness: 3: Some of the paper’s claims have minor issues. A few statements are not well-supported, or require small changes to be made correct.

display_title: I don't follow the w.l.o.g. claim in the main proof.

content.title: I don't follow the w.l.o.g. claim in the main proof.
content.comment:
In the proof sketch of the main theorem on page 4, the submission says

> We consider w.l.o.g. adjacent databases $D,D'\in\mathbb{R}^n$ with one-dimensional data instances $D = (0, \ldots , 0), D' = (1, 0, \ldots , 0)$.$^2$

This w.l.o.g. statement is key to the proof, but it is not obvious to me how to prove such a statement.

The full proof in the appendix does not provide further detail on this reduction. Footnote 2 on page 4 says

> This can be done w.l.o.g. by normalizing and performing unitary transform on the data instances. See also Appendix B.1 of Koskela et al. (2020).

I looked at [Appendix B.1. of Koskela et al.](https://proceedings.mlr.press/v108/koskela20b.html) and unfortunately I don't see how this relates to the claim here. We can apply an affine transformation to normalize general datasets, but once we shuffle the data items the affine transformation will no longer achieve the desired normalization. That is, the shuffle and the normalization don't "commute."

Can you please clarify how this w.l.o.g. claim is proved?

Thanks!

replying_to: Replying to I don't follow the w.l.o.g. claim in the main proof.

content.title: Thank you for the comment
content.comment:
Thanks for the insightful comment!

We have indeed overlooked the fact that normalization and shuffling do not "commute", and this makes the "wlog" argument invalid. 

Our main result is therefore correct only for the specific data structure in consideration, i.e., $D = (0,...,0); D' = (1,0,..,0)$, which cannot be applied to general use case like DP-SGD.

For now, we will withdraw our submission.
